The Papers Behind the Medicaid Question

Where Mom's deed, insurance policies and account records are, and who holds them.

Download PDF

The deed might be in the safe deposit box. The life insurance policy is somewhere in Mom's desk. Your brother has a folder he's been meaning to bring over.

This page doesn't ask you to understand any of these papers, or to work out what they mean for Medicaid. It asks where each one is, how recent it is, and who has it.

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it
The deed to Mom's home
A current property tax bill, and any mortgage or home loan statement
A recent statement for each account, showing the names on it
The deed or title for anything Mom owns with someone else
Trust documents, if there is a trust
Annuity contracts, with a recent statement for each
Life insurance policies
Any paperwork from a gift, a transfer or a change in ownership
What the hospital, the rehab or the facility has written about the care Mom needs
Papers that show where Mom lives and her citizenship or immigration status
Anything in writing you've been given about Medicaid: a handout, a letter, a note from the business office

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will look for it

Anything above with an empty line. Put a name next to each.

For example No copy of the deed. David will check the safe deposit box on Saturday. Nobody has the annuity contract; Karen will call the company and ask for a copy.

How to use it

  • Write the date printed on each paper. If it has no date, write “undated.”
  • Where a paper shows more than one name, copy the names exactly as they appear. Don't work out what they mean.
  • Don't rewrite or summarize a document here. Just say where it is.
  • Bring this page and the papers to your conversation with your Medicaid planner.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any deed, policy, trust or statement means, and it doesn't say which of them matter for Mom's situation. Medicaid rules vary by state, so that is a question for your Medicaid planner, and for an elder law attorney where a legal document is involved. Nothing here is legal, financial or tax advice.
